devices.title: CC1101 radio module
devices.summary: A radio link to Somfy RTS awnings.
devices.body:
# CC1101 radio module: wiring and setup

A CC1101 433 MHz transceiver, the Ebyte **E07-M1101D** with an SMA antenna socket, on an M5Stack
Atom Lite that runs ESPSomfy-RTS: the `awnings` component's node, which sends and hears Somfy RTS.
Device file: [cc1101.yaml](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/cc1101.yaml).

## Wiring

![E07-M1101D on an M5Stack Atom Lite: eight wires from G, 3V3, G22, G21, G33, G23, G19, G25 to module pins 1 to 8, and a 433 MHz antenna on the SMA socket](/wiring/cc1101-atom-lite.svg)

| E07-M1101D pin | signal | Atom Lite (bottom header) | wire | ESPSomfy-RTS, Radio page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | GND | G | black | |
| 2 | VCC | 3V3 (**never 5V**) | red | |
| 3 | GDO0 | G22 | purple | TX 22 |
| 4 | CSN | G21 | orange | CSN 21 |
| 5 | SCK | G33 | yellow | SCLK 33 |
| 6 | MOSI | G23 | blue | MOSI 23 |
| 7 | MISO | G19 | green | MISO 19 |
| 8 | GDO2 | G25 | white | RX 25 |

Pin 1 has the square pad. The pinout is the one the ESPSomfy-RTS wiki gives for this module; it is
the wiring of the first home's node. The Atom's 5V and the Grove port stay free. Another CC1101
board (a different maker) can number its pins differently: go by the signal names printed on it,
not by the numbers.

## The antenna

- Screw a **433 MHz** antenna onto the SMA socket before the node transmits. A CC1101 sending into
  an open socket can damage its output stage (general radio practice, not seen here).
- The antenna decides what the node hears. One home's wind sensor reached the node at −83 to
  −86 dBm and only part of its reports arrived, with gaps of hours (`components/awnings/README.md`).
  Stand the antenna upright and move the node, or the antenna on a short cable, towards the
  sensor and the awnings; keep it clear of metal.

## Firmware and first start

ESPSomfy-RTS is a release binary flashed over USB with `esptool`, then set up in its own web
page: the network, then on the Radio page the pins of the right-hand column above, then MQTT and a
virtual remote per awning. The commands and steps: `components/awnings/README.md`, "Flashing the
node". The radio answers when `GET http://<node>/controller` shows
`transceiver.config.radioInit: true`; `false` means the CC1101 did not answer on SPI with these pins
(a wire on the wrong socket, or VCC missing).

## When it does not work

| what you see | likely cause |
|---|---|
| `radioInit: false` | a wire on the wrong socket, the pins in ESPSomfy's Radio page not matching the wiring, or VCC not on 3V3 |
| awnings do not move, the node logs sending | no antenna, or the virtual remote not paired with the awning |
| the node hears the handsets only sometimes | reception: antenna position and distance |

The second and third rows are inference from how RTS works, apart from reception, which the first
home saw.

devices.title: HLK-LD2410C radar
devices.body:
# HLK-LD2410C radar: wiring and setup

A Hi-Link HLK-LD2410C 24 GHz presence radar on an M5Stack Atom Lite that already runs as a
`bermuda-presence` BLE proxy. It is that component's optional feature `radar`; the Ramka uses a
radar like this to wake its screen. Device file: [hlk-ld2410c.yaml](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/hlk-ld2410c.yaml).

## Wiring

![HLK-LD2410C on an M5Stack Atom Lite: 5V to VCC, G to GND, G22 to TX, G19 to RX, OUT not connected](/wiring/hlk-ld2410c-atom-lite.svg)

| Atom Lite (bottom header) | HLK-LD2410C | wire | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5V | VCC | red | the module needs 5 V; **never 3V3** |
| G | GND | black | |
| G22 | TX | purple | the Atom receives on G22 (`rx_pin: GPIO22`) |
| G19 | RX | green | the Atom sends on G19 (`tx_pin: GPIO19`) |
| — | OUT | — | not connected: presence comes over the UART |

Source: `components/bermuda-presence/esphome/ld2410.yaml`, the wiring of the first home's boards.
The labels are the ones printed on the Atom and on the module; the diagram shows which socket goes to
which pin, not where they sit on the boards. Colours are a convention: any colour works if both ends
match. The Grove port stays free.

## Firmware

The board's thin device file pulls the radar package next to the proxy package; with
`radar: true` on that proxy in the component's inputs, `domosenso add` writes it so (SPEC-015):

```yaml
packages:
  proxy: github://zerostorypoints/domosenso/components/bermuda-presence/esphome/ble-proxy.yaml@bermuda-presence/<version>
  radar: github://zerostorypoints/domosenso/components/bermuda-presence/esphome/ld2410.yaml@bermuda-presence/<version>
```

Then `esphome config`, `compile` and a flash, as for any proxy (`components/bermuda-presence/README.md`).
The UART runs at 256000 baud, the module's factory setting.

## After the first start

- The module keeps its settings (gates, thresholds, timeout, its own Bluetooth) in its own flash:
  set them once from Home Assistant; they survive a reflash of the Atom.
- Engineering mode is the one setting it forgets on a restart, and the light reading only comes in
  engineering frames, so the package switches it back on 10 s after every boot.
- New entities on the proxy's device: presence, moving and still target, detection distance and
  the others listed under `features.radar` in `components/bermuda-presence/component.yaml`.

## When it does not work

| what you see | likely cause |
|---|---|
| no radar entities at all | the device file lacks the `radar:` package line |
| radar entities `unavailable` or never changing | TX and RX swapped (TX must go to G22), or VCC on 3V3 |
| the Atom resets or drops off Wi-Fi when the radar is plugged in | a weak USB supply: the radar draws its power through the Atom; use a plain 5 V USB supply (the `power` note on `ble-proxy` in `components/bermuda-presence/component.yaml`) |
| presence that never clears with nobody there | sensitivity and gates, set from Home Assistant; the module keeps them |

The last two rows are inference from how the module and the board are powered and set up, not
cases seen in the first home.

The board runs the audio-sensor ESPHome package: a sound level every second and a third-octave spectrum (31 bands, 20 Hz to 20 kHz) about five times a second. It only measures; the package keeps the speaker amplifier off and adds no voice assistant or Bluetooth.

## Power and first flash

Power it from a plain 5 V USB supply. Flash it the first time over USB: hold the button while plugging in the cable, then run ESPHome with the device file the component writes for your home. Later updates go over Wi-Fi. Wi-Fi credentials and the API key stay in your private home project.

## Limits

It is not a measurement microphone: one analog MEMS capsule and one offset per board. One board has been tested in one home.

## Setup references

- [M5Stack Atom EchoS3R — M5Stack documentation](https://docs.m5stack.com/en/core/Atom_EchoS3R)

For Room presence, power the board from a plain 5 V USB supply and configure the ESPHome BLE proxy. Position proxies where Bluetooth coverage is needed. The optional radar has its own [wiring guide](/devices/hlk-ld2410c/).

devices.title: M5Stack Module CC1101 (868 MHz)
devices.summary: A radio link to a garage door or gate handset at 868 MHz.
devices.body:
# M5Stack Module CC1101 (868 MHz): wiring and setup

M5Stack's Module CC1101 (SKU M146): an Ebyte **E07-900M10S** (CC1101, 855 to 925 MHz) on an M-Bus
module with an SMA antenna socket, wired to an M5Stack Atom Lite with eight Dupont jumpers. The
`gate-remote` component's node, which captures and sends a gate handset's code at 868 MHz.
Device file: [m5stack-module-cc1101.yaml](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/m5stack-module-cc1101.yaml). For 433 MHz the other module,
[cc1101.md](/devices/cc1101/), has the same signals on the same Atom sockets.

## Wiring

![The module pin side up, antenna at the top, and the Atom from above: eight wires from G, 5V, G23, G19, G33, G21, G22, G25 to module pins 1, 28, 7, 9, 11, 8, 20, 22](/wiring/m5stack-cc1101-atom-lite.svg)

| Atom Lite socket | module M-Bus pin | label on the module's top side | signal | wire |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G | 1 | GND | ground | black |
| 5V | 28 | 5V | power | red |
| G23 | 7 | 23 | SPI MOSI | blue |
| G19 | 9 | 19 | SPI MISO | green |
| G33 | 11 | 18 | SPI clock | yellow |
| G21 | 8 | 25 | CSN | orange |
| G22 | 20 | 5 | GDO0, transmit data | purple |
| G25 | 22 | 13 | GDO2, receive data | white |

- **Power from 5V, never 3V3.** The module has its own regulator (VRH3301, 5 V → 3.3 V, M5Stack
  schematic SCH V0.1 2024-12-30); its M-Bus 3.3 V pin is not connected to anything.
- **The labels on the top side** are the GPIOs of M5Stack's Core controllers, not the Atom's: use
  them only to find a pin. Each pin goes through the board: a female socket on top, a short male pin
  underneath.
- **Pin columns on the pin side:** the column at the board edge holds the odd pins 1 to 29, pin 1 at
  the antenna end; the inner column the even pins 2 to 30. The module's printed "5V" arrow points at
  the inner column's 14th pin, which is pin 28. Before power, a continuity test from the antenna
  socket's shell must beep on the edge column's top three pins (1, 3, 5: ground).
- **Short pins.** Dupont sockets seat only part-way on the module's pins and can work loose. The node
  works that way (tested), but something that holds the eight housings is wise: the
  [enclosure](#enclosure) below, or a strip of tape.

## DIP switches

On the top side, next to a printed table. ON is the side printed "ON".

| switch | ON routes | set |
|---|---|---|
| SW1 1 | CSN to pin 8 | **ON** |
| SW1 2, 3, 4 | CSN to pins 23, 21, 24 | off |
| SW2 1, 2, 3 | GDO2 to pins 2, 22, 20 | **2 ON**, 1 and 3 off |
| SW2 4, 5, 6 | GDO0 to pins 2, 22, 20 | **6 ON**, 4 and 5 off |

GDO0 and GDO2 share the same three pins, so they must not be switched onto the same one.

## First start

Capture firmware and the steps: [components/gate-remote/README.md](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/components/gate-remote/README.md).
At boot the log shows `CC1101 found! Chip ID: 0x0014`; `Failed to verify CC1101.` means one of the SPI
wires or CSN does not seat. Tested with the SPI bus at 1 MHz over Dupont jumpers.

## Enclosure

![The closed enclosure: a grey box with the DomoSenso.org symbol, vent slots and a ring around the button well on its lid, the USB-C opening on the right and the antenna standing up at the back](/enclosures/m5stack-cc1101-atom-lite/closed.png)

A printable three-part box for the module, the Atom and the eight jumpers: a clamp held down by two
spring flaps in the lid keeps the female housings on the module's short pins. No supports, no
screws; the lid snaps on. The Atom's button sits at the bottom of a finger well, and the antenna
stands upright out of the back wall.

- [How to print and assemble it](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/enclosures/m5stack-cc1101-atom-lite/README.md): print settings,
  hardware, wiring, assembly, the parameters and what a first print has to confirm.
- Bambu Studio projects (P2S, settings applied): [base](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/enclosures/m5stack-cc1101-atom-lite/3mf/base.3mf),
  [base with wall ears](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/enclosures/m5stack-cc1101-atom-lite/3mf/base_wall.3mf),
  [lid](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/enclosures/m5stack-cc1101-atom-lite/3mf/lid.3mf),
  [clamp](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/enclosures/m5stack-cc1101-atom-lite/3mf/clamp.3mf).
- STL for other slicers: [base](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/enclosures/m5stack-cc1101-atom-lite/stl/base.stl),
  [base with wall ears](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/enclosures/m5stack-cc1101-atom-lite/stl/base_wall.stl),
  [lid](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/enclosures/m5stack-cc1101-atom-lite/stl/lid.stl),
  [clamp](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/enclosures/m5stack-cc1101-atom-lite/stl/clamp.stl),
  [ring and logo inlay](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/enclosures/m5stack-cc1101-atom-lite/stl/lid_inlay_parts.stl) (optional,
  second filament).
- [Parametric source](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/enclosures/m5stack-cc1101-atom-lite/enclosure.scad) (OpenSCAD).

Nothing has been printed yet: the dimensions come from M5Stack's drawings, and the model checks its
own fits and strains.

## The antenna

Screw an 868 MHz antenna onto the SMA socket before the node transmits (the module ships with a
2.5 dBi rubber antenna). A CC1101 sending into an open socket can damage its output stage (general
radio practice, not seen here).

devices.title: Shelly PM Mini Gen3
devices.summary: A small in-wall power meter behind the player's socket, read locally.
devices.body:
# Shelly PM Mini Gen3: wiring behind a socket

A small power meter for the wall box (model S3PM-001PCEU16). It sits in series with a socket's phase
and only measures: power, voltage, current and energy of what is plugged in. It does not switch.
Home Assistant reads it locally through the core `shelly` integration, without a cloud account.
In DomoSenso it is the `mains-meter` behind the music player: map its power and voltage sensors to
Ramka's `mains` input and the now-playing view shows the player's draw and voltage.
Device file: [shelly-pm-mini-gen3.yaml](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/devices/shelly-pm-mini-gen3.yaml).

## Wiring

![Shelly PM Mini Gen3 in a socket's wall box: the supply and onward phase meet in connector L, lead A goes to Shelly L, lead B from Shelly O to the socket's L; connector N feeds the socket's N (lead C) and Shelly N (lead D); the onward N and both PE stay in the socket](/wiring/shelly-pm-mini-gen3-socket.svg)

| lead | from | to |
|---|---|---|
| A | connector L (supply phase, onward phase) | Shelly L |
| B | Shelly O | socket L |
| C | connector N (supply neutral) | socket N |
| D | connector N | Shelly N |

- The onward phase, to the next socket on the circuit, joins in connector L, before the meter. Only
  what is plugged into this socket is measured; the next sockets are not.
- The onward neutral and both protective earths stay in the socket insert, as before.
- The two O terminals on the case are bridged inside; one is enough.
- Leads: short pieces of the supply's cross-section. The Shelly's screw terminals take 0.5 to 4 mm²,
  stripped 6 to 7 mm, at 0.4 Nm; the circuit breaker must be type B or C, 16 A at most (Shelly's
  specification). The connectors take the strip length printed on them.
- This is the wiring of the first home's meter, behind a multiple socket with a three-way lever
  connector for each of L and N. A socket with a switched outlet or a different terminal layout
  needs its own plan.

## Safety

Mains work. Switch off the circuit breaker and prove 0 V on L and N at the socket before touching a
wire. Have it done by a qualified electrician, or only as far as your local rules allow you to do it
yourself; some countries require an inspection afterwards. The drawing explains the connection, it
is not an installation approval.

## In Home Assistant

The `shelly` integration discovers the meter on the network. Check that the power and voltage
sensors update while the player is playing and in standby. The catalog recognises the meter by the
integration and a model name containing PM Mini (`domosenso recommend --from-ha`).

## Limits

One meter has been tested, in one home, behind one amplifier. Other metering Shelly models are
reported as likely mains meters, not as indexed devices.

## References

- [Shelly PM Mini Gen3 — Shelly knowledge base](https://kb.shelly.cloud/knowledge-base/shelly-pm-mini-gen3)
- [Shelly — Home Assistant](https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/shelly/)

devices.title: TCL wall tablet
devices.summary: Companion app, screen behavior and the tested landscape layout.
devices.body:
# Setting up the Ramka's tablet

From a reset Android tablet to the Ramka on screen, with the TCL NXTPAPER 11 Plus (9469X,
Android 16, `devices/tcl-9469x.yaml`) as the worked example. Other makers name the menus
differently; what each setting is for is said next to it, so the same switch can be found
elsewhere. The reasons behind the settings and the Companion app's quirks:
[the ramka field notes](https://github.com/zerostorypoints/domosenso/blob/b6e14f963a161b097976f66491d5b239e69f9739/components/ramka/README.md#the-tablet).

The paths for the screen lock, the WebView version, app pinning and the Companion app's own
settings were written down on the tested TCL. The others (system update, special app access,
developer options) are stock Android 16 paths, not checked on it. The `adb` line next to a setting
does the same from a computer, with USB debugging on (Settings → About tablet → tap *Build
number* seven times, then Settings → System → Developer options → *USB debugging*).

## 1. In Home Assistant, before the tablet

- **A user for the tablet.** Settings → People → Add person, *Allow login* on, *Administrator*
  off, *Can only log in from the local network* on if the tablet never leaves home. The tablet
  signs in as this user, never as you: the device and its entities get registered under it, and
  kiosk-mode hides the header and sidebar for this user only. Its user name goes into the
  `kiosk_user` input.
- **kiosk-mode** (optional): HACS → Frontend → *kiosk-mode* (NemesisRE). Without it the Ramka
  shows Home Assistant's header and sidebar. `?disable_km` on a URL shows them again.

## 2. Android

| what | where on the TCL | why | `adb` instead |
|---|---|---|---|
| Android updates | Settings → System → System update | the WebView below needs a current Android | — |
| *Android System WebView* 123 or newer | Play Store → update; the version: Settings → Apps → See all apps → Android System WebView, at the bottom | the cards import JSON modules; older WebViews do not load them | `adb shell dumpsys package com.google.android.webview \| grep versionName` |
| **Screen lock: None** | Settings → Security → Screen lock → None | the package wakes the screen; with a PIN or a swipe it stops on the lock screen | `adb shell locksettings set-disabled true` (only while no PIN is set) |
| NXTPAPER key: **Color Paper** | the NXTPAPER key at the right end of the top edge | Ink Paper turns photos and album art grey; Home Assistant cannot switch the mode | — |
| charge limit | none on this model; it stops at 80 % on the charger by itself | protects the battery on a tablet that never leaves the charger; on a tablet without a limit, use its battery-protection setting or a smart plug | — |

## 3. The Companion app

Install *Home Assistant* (`io.homeassistant.companion.android`) from the Play Store. 2026.8.4 or
newer if the Play Store offers it: 2026.6.5 can keep the screen on for good (field notes).

**Permissions**, Settings → Apps → Home Assistant (the app asks for the first two while it is set up;
if they were refused, they are under *Advanced* or Settings → Apps → Special app access):

| permission | value | without it | `adb` instead |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Modify system settings* | allowed | brightness and screen-timeout commands are dropped without a word | `adb shell appops set io.homeassistant.companion.android WRITE_SETTINGS allow` |
| *Display over other apps* | allowed | the app cannot come to the front after a wake; `app_importance` reads `cached` | `adb shell appops set io.homeassistant.companion.android SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW allow` |
| Battery → *Unrestricted* (battery optimisation **off**) | unrestricted | Android stops the app in the background and the commands stop arriving | `adb shell dumpsys deviceidle whitelist +io.homeassistant.companion.android` |
| Notifications | allowed | — | — |
| Location | may be denied | — | — |

**Sign in** to your Home Assistant's local URL as the tablet's user (section 1).

**App settings**, in the app: Settings → Companion app:

| setting | value | why |
|---|---|---|
| Device name | short, lower case, e.g. `ramka` | becomes `notify.mobile_app_<slug>` and `sensor.<slug>_*`, which go into the `tablet_device` input; set it before the first sign-in finishes, or rename the entities afterwards |
| **Keep screen on** | **off** | with it on the screen never sleeps; the package keeps the screen awake through Android's screen timeout instead |
| Fullscreen | on | hides Android's status and navigation bars |
| Screen orientation | Landscape | the tested layout is landscape |
| Always show first view on app start | on | after Android kills the app it comes back on the Ramka, not on the last page |
| Persistent connection | Always | commands arrive over the local websocket, not Firebase: no internet dependency, no delay |
| Manage sensors | on: `light_sensor`, `battery_level`, `app_importance`, `charger_type`, `battery_temperature`, `is_charging`; for your own view also `interactive`, `battery_state`, `battery_health` | the package reads the first six; a disabled sensor is missing from Home Assistant |
| Sensor update frequency | Fast always | once a minute; the slower settings drop to 15 minutes and brightness lags behind the room |

**Profile**, in the app as the tablet's user (the person icon at the bottom of the sidebar):
*Dashboard* = the Ramka's (`dashboard_path`, `dashboard-ramka` by default), *Language* and *Time
format* as the dashboard's language, *Theme* dark. Once kiosk-mode is active the profile page is
hidden: set these first, or open the profile with `?disable_km`.

**App pinning: leave it off.** Pinning (Settings → Security → App pinning) keeps a guest inside
the app, but it also blocks the way to unstick a screen that will not sleep (`command_launch_app`
to Android's Settings and back, field notes). The Ramka's Exit button on the controls is its way out
instead: a tap opens `exit_left`, a long press reloads the Ramka with kiosk-mode off.

## 4. Measure, render, check

1. `domosenso probe <target> --install`, open `<HA URL>/domosenso-probe/0` in the Companion app
   with the tablet in its final orientation, `domosenso probe <target> --read`, then
   `domosenso probe <target> --remove`. The `viewport` goes into the `screen` input; `webview`
   under 123 or `json-modules no` means the cards will not load; `user admin` means the app is
   signed in as an administrator (section 1).
2. Fill the inputs (`tablet_device`, `screen`, `kiosk_user`, the radar), render, deploy to staging,
   look at the shots, then production. Press `input_button.<prefix>_reload` once the tablet shows
   the dashboard.
3. With nobody near the radar for `off_delay_s` the screen goes dark; walking in wakes it on the
   ambient page. `sensor.<slug>_app_importance` reads `foreground` while the screen is on and
   `top_sleeping` while it sleeps.

| symptom | look at |
|---|---|
| the screen never sleeps | *Keep screen on* (section 3); on Companion 2026.6.5 see the field notes |
| it wakes onto the lock screen | Screen lock (section 2) |
| brightness never changes, the screen never times out | *Modify system settings* |
| it wakes on the launcher or another app, `app_importance` = `cached` | *Display over other apps* |
| commands arrive late or not at all after a while | battery *Unrestricted*, *Persistent connection* |
| a sensor the package needs is `unavailable` or missing | Manage sensors |
| the cards stay empty or show "Custom element doesn't exist" | the WebView version |
| English words on a Polish (or German) dashboard | the profile's language |


## A separate dashboard application

From Ramka 0.14.0, set the installation input `tablet_wake_package: com.domosenso.frame` when
Frame is the dashboard application. The default remains Home Assistant Companion. Keep Companion
installed, signed in and allowed to deliver its existing screen/launch notification commands.
Install and pair Frame separately before selecting it. Render, stage and review the deployment
plan, then verify a real radar wake restores the chosen app. Do not enable competing native radar
control when HA already owns sleep and brightness. This does not change any live HA preferences.

articles.title: How to add a Mi Flora plant sensor to Home Assistant
articles.summary: Set up Xiaomi BLE for a Flower Care sensor, troubleshoot discovery and missing battery readings, then check the data before adding plant reminders.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
For the **HHCCJCY01**, also sold as Flower Care or MiFlora, start with Home Assistant's
**Xiaomi BLE** integration. First get reliable readings into Home Assistant; then decide
how you want to display them or use them in a reminder.

## 1. Check Bluetooth reception

Home Assistant needs a working Bluetooth adapter or compatible Bluetooth proxy within range.
For initial setup, place the sensor close to the receiver. If you use an ESPHome proxy,
confirm that it is connected to Home Assistant before troubleshooting the plant sensor.
See the [Bluetooth integration guide](https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/bluetooth/)
for supported receivers and proxy arrangements.

## 2. Add Xiaomi BLE

The sensor should be discovered automatically. If necessary, open
**Settings → Devices & services → Add integration**, select **Xiaomi BLE** and follow
the setup steps. Some entities appear only after their first reading arrives.

## 3. Check firmware if discovery fails

Older firmware may not transmit the required Bluetooth advertisements. Home Assistant lists
**3.2.1** as the lowest confirmed working firmware version for this model.

If an update is needed, use the official Flower Care app and follow the linked firmware-update
instructions. The app and account are not required for ongoing Home Assistant operation
afterwards.

## 4. Give the battery reading time

Battery information requires an active Bluetooth connection. Home Assistant requests it only
once a day to conserve power, and reception must be strong enough for that connection.
Other readings arrive through passive broadcasts. A missing battery value therefore does not
necessarily mean that every part of the integration has failed.

These discovery, firmware and battery details come from the
[Home Assistant MiFlora documentation](https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/xiaomi_ble/#plant-sensor-flower-care-miflora-hhccjcy01).

## 5. Check the sensor in its final position

After setup, move the sensor to its intended pot and inspect the history over a normal watering
cycle. As a suggested acceptance check:

1. Give the device a name that identifies its pot.
2. Confirm that readings continue after it leaves the setup location.
3. Compare the moisture trend with your own observations of the soil.
4. Check whether gaps appear in the history before creating an alert.

Begin with a reminder you can evaluate. Do not choose one moisture threshold for every plant
simply because a dashboard makes it convenient. Record the plant, substrate and threshold you
choose in your own home project, so future adjustments have context.

## Use it with DomoSenso

The [Mi Flora device guide](/devices/mi-flora/) describes the readings to check before assigning
the sensor to a plant. The [plants component](/components/plants/) is the next step for the
framework's plant display. A sensor and a dashboard do not, by themselves, provide automatic
watering.

This article describes the upstream setup and a suggested check of your readings. It does
not claim a new hardware test or establish a watering threshold for your plants.

articles.title: How to set up a Bermuda Bluetooth proxy for room presence
articles.summary: Connect Bluetooth proxies, assign their rooms and check Bermuda's area estimates before building presence automations.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
A Bluetooth proxy receives nearby Bluetooth signals and forwards them to Home Assistant.
Bermuda uses those observations to estimate which room a device is in. The proxy provides
the observations; Bermuda interprets them.

This guide covers the upstream setup and a suggested acceptance check. It does not claim
that the procedure has been tested in your home.

## Before you start

Have Home Assistant running, compatible ESP32 hardware with Bluetooth proxy firmware, USB
power and a Bluetooth device you want to track. Start with two rooms so you can test a
transition between them. Home Assistant supports remote Bluetooth adapters through ESPHome;
the [Bluetooth integration documentation](https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/bluetooth/)
explains the supported arrangements.

## 1. Connect and name the proxies

Set up your ESP32 devices with ESPHome Bluetooth proxy firmware and add them to Home Assistant
through the ESPHome integration. Assign each proxy to the Home Assistant area where it is
physically installed. Choose names that make that assignment easy to check later.

## 2. Select a device in Bermuda

Follow the installation instructions in the
[Bermuda documentation](https://github.com/agittins/bermuda/wiki/). Open Bermuda's configuration
under **Settings → Devices & services** and select the Bluetooth device you want to track.
Bermuda supplies home/away tracking, an estimated area and distance sensors.

Phones that change their Bluetooth address may need additional identity handling. Bermuda
supports Home Assistant's Private BLE Device integration for compatible devices. Follow the
upstream instructions for your model rather than assuming that every phone or tracker
advertises a stable identity.

## 3. Check the room estimate

Before creating an automation, try this small acceptance exercise:

1. Leave the tracked device in the first room and record the reported area.
2. Carry it into the second room, wait for the estimate to settle and record the result.
3. Repeat with the device in a pocket and with doors closed.
4. Leave the device behind and walk out yourself.

That last step makes the limitation clear: the system is locating the device. A phone on
a desk remains there after its owner leaves.

## If the wrong room appears

First check the receiver's assigned area, its connection to Home Assistant and whether the
device is being detected. Keep a short record of locations that are confused. Try changing
one receiver position at a time, then repeat the same exercise. Treat the reported distance
as an estimate, not a measurement of the room.

Only build an automation after deciding what should happen when the device is left behind,
goes offline or changes rooms briefly. Start with a visible notification so you can inspect
the result before using it to control a room.

## Use it with DomoSenso

The [presence guide](/how-to/presence-who-is-home/) explains the framework's room-presence
approach and its optional radar hardware. The
[Bermuda presence component](/components/bermuda-presence/) records the released DomoSenso
scope. Keep proxy credentials and device identity information in your own home project.

articles.title: How to connect an M5Stack Atom EchoS3R to Home Assistant Assist
articles.summary: Check the hardware model, select the manufacturer's voice firmware and test each stage of a Home Assistant Assist command.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
Start by checking the exact model printed on your device. At the time of writing, M5Stack's
documentation at the Atom EchoS3R guide URL uses the name **Atom VoiceS3R**. Match your hardware
to the manufacturer's product page before choosing firmware.

This is a guide to the manufacturer's Assist setup, not a claim of a tested DomoSenso voice
integration. DomoSenso currently documents this board as an
[audio sensor](/devices/m5stack-atom-echos3r/): its package measures sound and keeps the speaker
amplifier off. That package does not add a voice assistant or Bluetooth. Installing voice
firmware is a different use of the device; do not assume both functions will keep running.

## 1. Prepare the voice pipeline

Choose the Assist pipeline the satellite will use. The manufacturer documents both Home
Assistant Cloud and a local pipeline. Test your chosen pipeline in Home Assistant first,
so you have a working reference before adding the satellite.

## 2. Install firmware for the correct hardware

Use the precompiled firmware or complete ESPHome configuration linked from the
[manufacturer's setup guide](https://docs.m5stack.com/en/homeassistant/applications/voice_assistant/atom_echos3r).
The guide currently specifies ESPHome **2026.1.0 or later**. Check that requirement again
when preparing your device.

Use the complete configuration rather than mixing microphone and speaker settings from
similarly named Atom models. Save the configuration and firmware revision you use, along with
the ESPHome version. If this device already performs another job, preserve its configuration
before replacing its firmware.

## 3. Add the satellite to Home Assistant

Once the device joins your network, accept its ESPHome discovery prompt and assign it to an
area. Open its voice assistant settings, then choose its area and Assist pipeline.

The manufacturer's example uses **Okay Nabu** as its wake word. Begin with one exposed light
and a clear command, then check that you can hear the response.

## 4. Find the stage that fails

Use this sequence as a troubleshooting worksheet:

| Observation | Next check |
| --- | --- |
| The device is offline | Check power and network connection before changing voice settings. |
| The device is online but does not react | Confirm the selected firmware and configured wake word. |
| It reacts but the command fails | Compare the result with the same request in the working Assist pipeline. |
| The action succeeds but there is no audible reply | Check the response and audio-output stages separately. |

Change one thing at a time and repeat the same command. A clear description such as
“the light turns on but no response is audible” is more useful than “voice does not work”.

## Choose the job before choosing the package

For voice interaction, follow the upstream Assist configuration above. For room sound readings,
read the [DomoSenso audio-sensor component](/components/audio-sensor/) and its stated limits.
These are separate configurations, and this article does not establish that they can be combined.

articles.title: Stop on a page and read it
articles.summary: Ramka 0.9.0 pauses the rotation from the bottom-right corner and turns plant pages and photos with a sideways swipe. Ramka 0.8.0 and 0.9.0 also bring a list of every plant, climate widgets, named colours, a preview dashboard and a Live visualization switch.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
Ramka 0.8.0 was tagged on 31 October 2026 and 0.9.0 on 1 November. This article covers both.

## Pause and swipe

On the wall, a tap anywhere opens the controls, so there was no way to stay on a page long enough to read it. In 0.9.0 the bottom-right corner of the rotation pauses it: the page on screen and the view inside it stay, and a small play button in that corner resumes the rotation with the page's full time. A sideways swipe steps through the views of the page on screen: the plant pages, or the photos of the current series, round in both directions. Climate, air and status have one view and ignore it. Up and down still turn the pages. While paused, every swipe keeps the pause, and the controls give back the paused page when they close. The pause ends when the screen goes off, so the next person who walks up gets the rotation.

## Every plant on one page

With more than four plants, a list page now follows the tile pages: one row per plant with its photo, name, room, action, the sun, fertiliser and water bars and the moisture line, up to seven rows a page. A plant without a photo shows a leaf in its state's colour instead of its initial.

## Climate widgets and named colours

The climate page holds up to twenty widgets: temperature, air quality, custom (any two readings) or an empty tile, in an order you drag into place on the settings dashboard. Colour settings pick from one list of named colours that follows the theme, shown with a dot in each choice. The air page's levels read good, fair and poor, and their colours are set on the Air page.

## Settings and a preview

Every settings page opens with what its screen shows and when. Controls on approach and the near settings have their own Controls page. A new preview dashboard, on by default, shows each screen in a frame of the tablet's size, so a setting can be checked without waiting for the rotation. An About page lists the components a home runs and their links.

## The music visual

The visual now has its own switch, Live visualization, off by default: every home starts on the classic wave and switches it on in the settings. Response profiles set how the visual moves, and the Behind speakers EQ preset is a measured curve rather than flat. The Live visualization page reads the music sensor's abilities from audio-sensor's music source, released the same day in audio-sensor 0.3.0, which also brings a six-range EQ to the music cards and needs no new flash. Update the two together: with audio-sensor 0.2.0 that page cannot tell what the sensor can do.

## Upgrade deliberately

`domosenso update ramka` moves the cards to the new version's folder; then deploy and press the Ramka's reload button. Add the preview dashboard's entry, or set `preview_dashboard: false`. A script that reset the near settings with `page: general` passes `page: controls` now. The Ramka component page links the upgrade notes for both releases.

articles.title: Ramka finds the plants itself
articles.summary: Ramka 0.7.0 shows 1 to 50 plants in pages, with plants 0.3.1 saying when each was watered and when it will need water. Ramka 0.5.0 and 0.6.0 bring more settings, and audio-sensor 0.2.0 a faster spectrum.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
Three Ramka releases, two plants releases and an audio-sensor release were tagged on 30 and 31 October 2026. This article covers them together.

## Plants, from one to fifty

With plants 0.3.0, each plant carries its room, its limits, an optional photo and its names, so Ramka 0.7.0 can find every plant with `plants: discover` instead of a list in its inputs. The plants page shows up to six plants at a time by default, the tiles growing to fill the screen; with more plants, pages turn every ten seconds, the plants that need something first, with one dot per plant grouped by room. A tile shows the photo or the plant's initial, its 7-day moisture line and, from plants 0.3.0, "watered N days ago" or "water in ~N days". The colours are green, grey and amber, never red. Plants per page and time per page are on the settings dashboard.

Plants 0.3.0 also lists a moisture sensor that sits in soil but belongs to no plant, so a new probe in a pot is noticed. Plants 0.3.1 fixes two faults found on the first home: "water in" was never known because the drying rate was rounded to zero, and the new-sensor notice was disabled at start.

## More settings without a render

Ramka 0.5.0 adds settings pages for Photos (albums, photos per series, time per photo), Air (each reading and its two limits), Climate (the rooms and their readings) and Calendar, plus a General page. Ramka 0.6.0 raises the Climate rooms from five to ten.

## A faster spectrum

audio-sensor 0.2.0 follows a bass hit in about 0.3 s instead of up to about 1 s. The board has three update rates; with Ramka 0.6.0 it runs on the fast one only while the music view is on screen and returns to normal afterwards. The faster rate needs the board flashed with the 0.2.0 firmware; until then the spectrum keeps its old pace.

## Upgrade deliberately

Update plants to 0.3.1 before, or in the same deploy as, Ramka 0.7.0 when you switch to `plants: discover`; before plants 0.3.0 runs, the page says there are no plants. A plant list in Ramka's inputs keeps working. Update audio-sensor together with Ramka 0.6.0 or later. The component pages link each release's upgrade notes.

articles.title: Ramka draws the music in the room
articles.summary: Ramka 0.4.0 can show the room's sound on the now-playing page, and every setting is now live.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
Ramka 0.4.0 and the new audio-sensor component are released together. A small M5Stack Atom EchoS3R board in the room measures the sound level and a third-octave spectrum; with `music_visual: spectrum` or `level`, the now-playing page draws that measurement in its wave strip instead of the classic wave. Without a reading, the strip falls back to the classic wave.

## Settings without a render

Every behaviour setting of Ramka is now a Home Assistant helper the tablet reads live. A new admin dashboard, "Ramka settings", has one page per view plus General: which pages rotate, presence and display timing, the theme and the music visual's look. A change reaches the tablet within about a second. "Reset to defaults" returns a page to its starting values.

## Upgrade deliberately

0.4.0 includes 0.3.1, which brings the clock card's forecast back after a Home Assistant restart. One step is required: add the settings dashboard's `lovelace:` entry to your `configuration.yaml`. A home that already runs Ramka keeps its tuned presence and display values. The visual needs audio-sensor with one board marked `music: true`; flashing the board the first time is done over USB.

The audio sensor is not a measurement microphone: it has one capsule and one calibration offset per board, and it has been tested with one board in one home. Read the upgrade notes linked below before changing a live installation.

Both releases were merged and tagged on 30 October 2026.

articles.title: Try it before it reaches your home
articles.summary: Every change can now be opened in a local Home Assistant first, by anyone, without writing code.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
DomoSenso now has a shared way of working that is open to anyone. Contributors use a fork and run the same checks as the core team. An AI agent reviews each change, and a human approves it. Nobody can approve their own pull request, and that includes the maintainers.

## Look at a pull request before it is accepted

Ask Codex or Claude Code to run `preview-pr` for a pull request number. It starts a fictional home on your computer with the real Ramka on screen. You can switch it between morning, evening, away and rain. It has no lights, speakers or blinds of its own; light switches and music commands are only recorded. When you have seen enough, you accept the change or ask for changes.

## Test an update on your own home

`stage-home-update` does the same for your own home. It sets up a separate Home Assistant with no access to your network or the internet, and with none of your passwords. It loads the configuration you have now, then the update, and compares the two. In the first run on a real home, three component updates went through and every entity, automation and dashboard came out the same. The only difference was the new address of the Ramka's cards.

## Still to come

A test Home Assistant starts empty, so the tiles on the dashboards have no readings. Next it will be able to show real readings copied from your own Home Assistant, or realistic invented ones when none are available.

articles.title: From a component to the wires
articles.summary: Two documented Atom connections, plus the tablet setup they help support.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
Hardware requirements should lead to instructions you can inspect.

The [HLK-LD2410C radar guide](/devices/hlk-ld2410c/) pairs a labeled wiring diagram with a pin table, firmware steps and first-start checks. The [CC1101 guide](/devices/cc1101/) does the same for the radio node used with Somfy RTS awnings.

## Same board, different jobs

The radar accompanies an ESPHome Bluetooth proxy. The CC1101 radio node runs ESPSomfy-RTS. These are distinct firmware roles; one board should not be presented as doing both jobs at once.

## Finish at the screen

The [tablet setup guide](/devices/tcl-9469x/) covers the Companion app and Android settings used by the documented Ramka installation. Wiring, firmware, integration and presentation are separate steps, and each needs a check.

These guides describe the documented models and connections. They do not establish support for all related boards, radios or meters.

articles.title: Keep only the pages you need
articles.summary: The status page can now be removed from Ramka’s ambient rotation.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
Ramka 0.3.0 adds `status_page: false`. It removes the read-only status page from both the rotation and the swipe sequence. Status remains enabled by default.

## When to use it

If the controls already show your lights and awnings, and there are no other status items you want to see, the extra ambient page may add little. You can keep the useful pages and leave that one out.

Climate, air, plants and photos still depend on their own inputs. At least one ambient page must remain; a render with no ambient pages fails rather than leaving an empty rotation.

## Upgrade deliberately

Review the release notes linked below. Update the component in your separate home project, adjust the inputs, render and inspect the resulting pages. Review the deployment plan before changing a live installation.

The release was merged on 27 October 2026. This article’s publication date is 28 October; it is not the tag creation date.

articles.title: A tablet, a radar, an ordinary shelf
articles.summary: Inside the maintainer’s first installation: components with a physical home.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
The first installation brings an Android tablet, a nearby radar and Home Assistant together. This is the maintainer’s personal setup, not a customer project. The photographs were already published in the original installation journal.

## Give the screen a reason to wake

Ramka supplies the ambient pages and controls. The radar supplies presence and distance through the optional radar feature of Room presence. Bluetooth room estimates and radar presence are separate signals; the screen does not need to identify a person to react to someone nearby.

## Show what is already happening

The media integration supplies a Home Assistant media player. Ramka can use its track metadata for the now-playing view. The documented player is a Hegel H400; a speaker visible in a photograph is not a claim about compatibility.

## What this installation taught us

A wall display needs more than a dashboard layout. Screen wake and sleep, Android permissions, charging behavior and the viewport all matter. The [tablet guide](/devices/tcl-9469x/) records the tested setup; the [radar guide](/devices/hlk-ld2410c/) records the wiring.

The original journal documented Ramka 0.2.0. This article does not establish which version is running in the home today. Field experience remains limited; another installation needs its own validation.

articles.title: A dashboard should fit the home it lives in
articles.summary: Ramka 0.2.0 made climate, air, plants and photos conditional on your inputs.
articles.author: DomoSenso
articles.body:
Not every home has plant sensors. Not every tablet needs a photo album.

In Ramka 0.2.0, climate, air, plants and photos became optional. Leave out an input and the corresponding page is left out of the rendered dashboard and its rotation. The shared component stays the same; each home decides what belongs on its screen.

## Before upgrading

Read the pinned release notes below, review your inputs and render the dashboard before applying changes. This historical article retains the date and subject of the original homepage entry. The [current component page](/components/ramka/) may describe a newer release.
